title: Purim: turned upside down (Esther 9:1)
hookLine: on the very day meant for destruction, everything is reversed
tomorrow: Purim: two gifts to the poor

lines: PUR: A LOT CAST FOR A DAY.
cards: Haman, the king's chief minister, wants every Jew in the empire dead. To choose the day, he casts lots, and the lot falls on the thirteenth of Adar, nearly a year away.

That lot, in Hebrew pur, gives the holiday its name: Purim, lots. The book of Esther is full of plans that go exactly the wrong way for the person making them. Haman builds a tall gallows for Mordecai.

He walks into the palace expecting honor and ends up leading Mordecai through the streets on the king's horse, shouting his praises. And by chapter nine, the book has a two-word Hebrew phrase for all of it.

teach.b: Chapter nine opens on the thirteenth of Adar itself, the day Haman chose. The enemies of the Jews had hoped, the text says, to rule over them. And then: v'nahafoch hu.
It was turned around. Upside down. Instead, the Jews ruled over those who hated them.
In Hebrew the phrase is almost a shrug: and it turned over. And it's the hinge of the whole book.
Haman is hanged on the gallows he built. Mordecai wears the royal robes Haman wanted for himself.
The day of destruction becomes a day of rescue, and the month of grief, the book says a few verses later, becomes a month of gladness. The Talmud adds a reversal of its own.
In tractate Megillah, it says Haman was delighted when the lot fell in Adar, because Moses died in Adar. What he didn't know, the Talmud says, is that Moses was also born in Adar.
Purim turns this idea into how the day feels.
When Haman's name is read, synagogues fill with the noise of rattles and stamping feet. Some communities appoint a Purim rabbi who makes fun of the real one.
The Talmud even says one should drink on Purim until one can't tell cursed is Haman from blessed is Mordecai, a line rabbis have debated ever since, and some read far more gently than it sounds.
For a day, the world is allowed to stand on its head, because once, on a very bad day, it did.

how: On Purim, the fourteenth of Adar (the fifteenth in walled cities like Jerusalem), Jews hear the book of Esther read aloud at night and in the morning, making noise at Haman's name, and many wear costumes and hold a festive meal.

o: and they rested: the feast after the battle
and the lot was cast: a day chosen by chance
and it was turned around: the plot reversed

games.q: inside the great reversal — tap the pairs.
p: a lot, cast to choose the day

s: Purim is named for the lots Haman cast
Haman chose the date by consulting the king
he cast lots, and the lot fell on the thirteenth of Adar.
the Talmud says Haman didn't know Moses was born in Adar
he was glad Moses died in Adar, not knowing Moses was also born then.

games.q: you're Haman. the king asks what should be done for the man he wants to honor. you're sure he means you. what do you suggest?
o: royal robes, the king's horse, and a herald.
a seat at the king's right hand.
games.why: Haman asks for the royal robes, the king's horse and a herald, and then has to give them all to Mordecai. the reversals begin.

practice: Go back over the last few years and find one moment that looked like a disaster when it happened: a rejection, a move, a plan that fell apart. Then trace what grew out of it that you wouldn't give back.
You don't have to call it a miracle; just notice the turn.

wordCard.voice: V'nahafoch hu. It was turned upside down: the hinge of the book of Esther, and the feeling of Purim. Today's word.
